caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Latvia's debt went from 10.7% of GDP in 2006 (9% in 2007, the low) to 48.2% in 2010, the series peak, on the IMF-EU bailout and the banking rescue — one of the sharpest increases in Europe. It then stabilized: 44% in 2020, 44.4% in 2022, and a projected 46.9% in 2025. The internal-devaluation strategy preserved the euro peg (adopted January 2014) at the cost of a deep output collapse. GDP grew from $20.4bn in 2006 to a projected $48.6bn in 2025. Debt is moderate and sustainable; the legacy is a smaller, more flexible economy.
inflation_management: Latvia had Europe's most extreme boom-bust inflation cycle: 15.3% in 2008 on the credit boom, then -1.2% in 2010 (the low) during internal devaluation. Euro adoption in 2014 brought ECB policy; inflation was 0.1% in 2020, then 17.2% in 2022, the series high — among the eurozone's highest on energy exposure. It fell to 1.3% in 2024, projected 3.8% for 2025. The fixed-exchange-rate regime (first the peg, then the euro) has always meant adjustment through domestic prices, for better and worse.

key_events.event: Severe boom-bust: IMF-EU bailout (December 2008); internal devaluation defended the peg through a deep contraction.
Debt peaked at 48.2% of GDP as bailout costs landed.
Joined the euro area (January 2014), completing the post-crisis normalization.
COVID-19: moderate fiscal response; debt at 44% of GDP.
Energy shock: inflation hit 17.2%, the series high; Latvia fronted the EU's Russia sanctions push.

outlook_next_decade: Latvia's macro framework is sound — euro membership, moderate debt, flexible markets — but the structural challenges are demographic decline, emigration, and the security environment. Defense spending and energy-transition costs will keep some fiscal pressure. Inflation should normalize toward the ECB target as the 2022-23 energy effects fully wash out. The base case is steady convergence growth; the security situation is the dominant risk to the outlook, not macroeconomics.
